lessons.title: Types of Waste: Municipal, Industrial, Electronic, Organic
lessons.body: Waste is not just 'garbage'âit comes in distinct streams, each with its own source, composition, and handling needs. Municipal solid waste (MSW) is what households, schools, and markets throw away daily. In African cities, MSW is often 50-60% organic matter (food scraps, leaves), 10-15% plastics, 5-10% paper, and the rest metals, glass, and textiles. Industrial waste comes from factories, workshops, and construction sites: scrap metal, sawdust, chemical sludge, and offcuts. Electronic waste (e-waste) includes old phones, computers, TVs, and batteriesâgrowing fast as Africa's tech use rises. Organic waste is biodegradable material from kitchens, gardens, and farms. Knowing these differences matters because each stream needs a different recycling method. For example, you can compost organic waste in 30-60 days, but plastics need sorting by resin type before processing. Start by observing your own community: visit a local dump, a market, and a repair shop. Count what you see. You'll quickly learn that 'waste' is actually a mix of valuable resources waiting to be separated.

lessons.title: Material Identification: Plastics, Metals, Glass, Paper
lessons.body: To recycle, you must first identify materials correctly. Plastics are marked with a resin code (1-7) inside a triangle. PET (1) is clear and used for soda bottles; HDPE (2) is opaque and used for milk jugs; PVC (3) is rigid and used for pipes; LDPE (4) is flexible and used for bags; PP (5) is tough and used for buckets; PS (6) is brittle and used for disposable cups; and 'other' (7) includes mixed plastics. A simple test: squeeze the plasticâif it cracks easily, it's likely PS (6); if it bends, it's PP (5) or LDPE (4). Metals: use a magnet. Steel and iron stick; aluminium, copper, and brass do not. Aluminium cans are lightweight and shiny; copper wires are reddish and heavy. Glass: check colour and thickness. Clear, green, and brown glass are common. Glass is 100% recyclable infinitely, but mixed colours lower value. Paper: tear it. Long fibres (like in cardboard) are stronger; short fibres (like newspaper) are weaker. Office paper is white and high-grade; newspaper is grey and low-grade. In Africa, informal collectors often sort by handâtrain your eye and hands to recognise these quickly. A good tool is a simple sorting chart with pictures, laminated and hung at your collection point.

lessons.title: Waste Audits: How to Conduct a Business Waste Assessment
lessons.body: A waste audit tells you exactly what your business throws away, how much, and where it goes. It takes one day and costs almost nothing. Step 1: Pick a typical dayâavoid holidays. Step 2: Collect all waste from bins in labelled bags (e.g., 'office', 'kitchen', 'workshop'). Step 3: Weigh each bag using a hanging scale (accurate to 0.1 kg). Step 4: Open each bag on a tarp and sort into categories: organic, plastics, paper, metals, glass, e-waste, hazardous, and other. Step 5: Weigh each category separately. Step 6: Record everything in a table. For example, a small restaurant might find: 40 kg organic, 5 kg plastics, 3 kg paper, 2 kg glass, 1 kg metals per day. That's 51 kg total. Step 7: Calculate percentages. If organic is 78%, composting could cut waste by more than three-quarters. Step 8: Identify recyclables with market value. In Nairobi, PET bottles fetch 20-30 KES per kg; scrap metal 30-50 KES per kg. Step 9: Set a targetâe.g., reduce landfilled waste by 50% in three months. Repeat the audit monthly to track progress. This data helps you negotiate with recyclers and design better collection systems.

lessons.title: Hazardous Waste: Identification and Safe Handling
lessons.body: Hazardous waste can harm people, animals, and the environment. Common hazardous items in Africa include: batteries (lead-acid, lithium), fluorescent tubes (mercury), paints and solvents, pesticides, medical waste (syringes, expired drugs), and electronic components (circuit boards with heavy metals). How to identify? Look for warning symbols: skull and crossbones (toxic), flame (flammable), corrosion symbol (acid), and exclamation mark (irritant). If unsure, treat it as hazardous. Safe handling rules: 1) Never mix hazardous with regular waste. 2) Wear gloves, goggles, and a mask. 3) Store in sealed, labelled containersânever in food or drink bottles. 4) Keep away from water sources and children. 5) For batteries, tape terminals to prevent sparks. 6) For medical waste, use sharp-safe boxes and incinerate or autoclave if available. 7) For e-waste, do not burn cables to recover copperâthis releases toxic fumes. 8) Contact local authorities or specialised recyclers. In many African countries, hazardous waste collection is limited, so businesses should partner with certified handlers. For example, in South Africa, the National Waste Management Strategy requires safe disposal. If no service exists, store securely until a solution is found. Never dump hazardous waste in rivers or open pits.

lessons.title: Composting Organic Waste: Methods and Benefits
lessons.body: Composting turns food scraps and garden waste into nutrient-rich soil. It reduces waste by up to 60% and saves money on fertiliser. Method 1: Pit composting. Dig a pit 1m deep, 1m wide, 1m long. Add alternating layers of 'greens' (kitchen scraps, fresh leaves) and 'browns' (dry leaves, cardboard, sawdust) in a 1:2 ratio. Keep moist like a wrung-out sponge. Turn every 2 weeks. Ready in 2-3 months. Method 2: Heap composting. Build a pile 1.5m high on a shaded spot. Same layering. Cover with a tarp to retain moisture. Turn weekly. Ready in 6-8 weeks. Method 3: Vermicomposting. Use a bin with red wiggler worms. Feed them fruit and vegetable scraps (no meat, dairy, or citrus). Worms produce castings in 4-6 weeks. Great for small spaces. Benefits: compost improves soil water retention by 20-30%, increases crop yields by 20-50%, and reduces methane from landfills. In Africa, composting is low-cost: a family can compost 5-10 kg of waste per week. Use the compost for urban gardens, tree nurseries, or sell itâa 50 kg bag can fetch 500-1000 KES. Avoid composting meat, bones, oily foods, and diseased plants. Keep the pile aerated to prevent smell. Composting is a simple business: collect organic waste from markets, compost, and sell to farmers.

lessons.title: E-Waste: Challenges and Opportunities in Recycling
lessons.body: Electronic waste (e-waste) is the fastest-growing waste stream in Africa. Each year, the continent generates over 3 million tonnes, with only 10-15% formally recycled. Challenges: 1) Informal recyclingâburning cables and open-pit acid baths to recover copper and goldâexposes workers to toxic fumes and soil contamination. 2) Lack of collection infrastructureâmost e-waste ends up in dumps or is stored in homes. 3) Data securityâdiscarded devices may contain personal information. 4) Low awarenessâmany people don't know e-waste is hazardous. Opportunities: 1) Refurbishmentârepair and resell working devices. A used laptop can be refurbished for 5,000-10,000 KES and sold for 15,000-25,000 KES. 2) Component recoveryâextract gold, silver, copper, and aluminium from circuit boards. One tonne of circuit boards contains 40-800 times more gold than one tonne of gold ore. 3) Plastics recyclingâe-waste plastics can be shredded and moulded into new products. 4) Training and jobsâe-waste recycling creates 10-20 times more jobs per tonne than landfilling. To start: set up a collection point, partner with certified recyclers (e.g., in Kenya, the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Centre), and promote 'take-back' schemes. Always use protective gear and avoid burning. E-waste is not just a problemâit's a business waiting to be built.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Running a Waste Audit and Building a Green Business in Africa

For an African SME, waste is rarely just an environmental issue â it is a cost line, a compliance risk, and often an untapped revenue stream. A bakery in Kumasi, a print shop in Nairobi, or a hotel in Lagos all generate predictable waste streams that can be measured, reduced, and in some cases sold. This Practical Reference lesson gives you the tools to assess what your business throws away, identify materials with resale value, handle hazardous fractions safely, and turn the findings into a bankable green business plan.

The starting point is always the same: you cannot manage what you have not measured. A waste audit turns guesswork into data. From that data you can negotiate better collection contracts, design a composting or recycling side-line, or simply stop paying for disposal of materials that someone else will pay you for.

Why the Audit Comes First

Collection fees in many African cities are charged by volume or by bin size, not by weight. That means the cheapest win is usually reducing volume â flattening cardboard, separating organics, or baling plastics. A three-day audit of your normal operations will typically reveal that 40â70% of what you pay to have hauled away is either organic material that could be composted on site or clean recyclables that a local aggregator will buy.

Step-by-Step Waste Audit for a Small Business

  1. Define the boundary. One site, one week, all shifts. Include kitchen, production floor, office, and yard.
  2. Map the generation points. Walk the site and mark every bin, skip, and dumping spot on a simple sketch.
  3. Collect for 3â7 days. Label separate bags per stream: organics, plastics, paper, metals, glass, e-waste, hazardous, mixed.
  4. Weigh or estimate. A hanging scale or bathroom scale is enough. Record weight and volume (bin height filled).
  5. Photograph and log. Take photos of each bag. Note contamination (food in plastics, batteries in general waste).
  6. Calculate cost per stream. Multiply volume by your collection tariff, or weight by the local tipping fee.
  7. Identify market value. Call local recyclers, scrap dealers, and compost buyers. Get current prices per kg.
  8. Set targets and actions. E.g. divert 60% of organics to on-site compost within 90 days.

Data Table 1: Waste Streams, Risks, and Business Opportunities

Stream Typical Sources Main Risk Business Opportunity

Industrial Factories, workshops Chemical residues, permits By-product recovery, scrap metal
Electronic (e-waste) IT, repair shops, households Toxicity, informal burning Refurbishment, parts, certified recycling
Organic Markets, kitchens, farms Methane, odour, pests Compost, animal feed, biogas
Plastics Packaging, retail, industry Marine litter, low value mixed Flakes, pellets, paving blocks
Metals Construction, workshops Theft, injury High resale value, scrap trade
Glass Hospitality, bottling Cuts, weight Crushing, re-melt, aggregate
Paper Offices, print, packaging Moisture, contamination Baling, pulp, egg trays
Hazardous Clinics, garages, labs Health, legal liability Licensed collection contracts

Sources: Adapted from UNEP (2015) Global Waste Management Outlook; Kaza et al. (2018) What a Waste 2.0, World Bank; and Basel Convention Secretariat guidance on hazardous waste classification.

Material Identification: What to Look For

In practice, African recyclers pay for clean, sorted, dry material. Mixed or wet loads are rejected or discounted. Learn the resin codes on plastics (1 PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 4 LDPE, 5 PP, 6 PS, 7 Other). PET bottles and HDPE jerrycans have the strongest local demand. Metals are the highest-value stream â aluminium, copper, and brass command the best prices per kg. Glass is heavy and low-value unless you have a local crusher or bottle-washer. Paper must be kept dry; a single rain-soaked bale can be worthless.

Data Table 2: Indicative Waste Volumes and Diversion Potential by Business Type

Business Type Dominant Stream Approx. Share of Total Waste Realistic Diversion Target Likely Payback Route
Restaurant / hotel Food organics 55â70% 60â80% composted Reduced collection fees; compost sales
Market / grocery Organic + cardboard 60â75% 50â70% Compost, baling paper
Office / bank Paper + e-waste 50â65% paper 70â90% Secure shredding, IT refurb
Print / packaging Paper + plastics 70â85% 75â90% Baling, offcut resale
Garage / workshop Metals + used oil 40â60% metal 80â95% metal Scrap metal, licensed oil collection
Clinic / pharmacy Hazardous + packaging 20â35% hazardous 100% hazardous to licensed handler Compliance; avoid fines

Sources: Ranges synthesised from UNEP Global Waste Management Outlook (2015); World Bank What a Waste 2.0 (2018); and country-level waste characterisation studies published by the African Clean Cities Platform (ACCP). Figures are indicative and vary by city and season.

Hazardous Waste: Identification and Safe Handling

Hazardous waste is any material that is toxic, flammable, corrosive, reactive, or infectious. In African SMEs the most common fractions are used motor oil and filters, solvents and paints, batteries (lead-acid and lithium), fluorescent tubes, medical sharps and expired pharmaceuticals, and e-waste components such as CRTs and circuit boards. These must never enter general waste, open burning, or informal dumping. They require licensed handlers, manifest documentation, and in many countries a permit from the national environmental authority (e.g. NEMA in Kenya, NESREA in Nigeria, EPA in Ghana).

â  SAFETY WARNING â HAZARDOUS WASTE

Never burn, bury, or mix hazardous waste with general refuse. Batteries, e-waste, solvents, and medical waste release toxic fumes and leach into soil and groundwater. Always wear gloves, eye protection, and a dust mask when handling. Store in labelled, sealed, leak-proof containers on a bunded surface away from drains and food. Use only licensed hazardous waste contractors and keep signed manifests for at least three years. In case of spill or exposure, contact your national environmental authority and local emergency services immediately. Uncontrolled hazardous waste is a criminal offence in most African jurisdictions.

Composting Organic Waste: Methods and Benefits

Given that organics are the largest fraction of African municipal waste, composting is usually the fastest route to measurable diversion. Three practical methods suit SMEs:

  • Static pile / windrow: Best for markets, farms, and landscapers. Turn weekly; aim for 55â65Â°C core temperature. Ready in 8â12 weeks.
  • Three-bin system: Ideal for hotels and restaurants with limited space. Rotate bins, harvest finished compost monthly.
  • Bokashi / vermicompost: Suits small kitchens and urban rooftops. Fast, low-odour, produces high-value worm castings.

Benefits go beyond disposal savings: compost improves soil fertility, reduces chemical fertiliser costs for landscapers and farms, and can be sold in 50 kg bags to urban gardeners. Keep the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio near 25â30:1 by mixing food waste with dry leaves, sawdust, or shredded cardboard.

E-Waste: Challenges and Opportunities

Africa generates a growing volume of e-waste, both domestically and through imports. The challenges are well documented: informal dismantling, open burning of cables, acid leaching for gold, and child labour. The opportunities are equally real. Refurbishment and repair create jobs and extend device life. Recovering copper, aluminium, gold, and rare earths from printed circuit boards is high-value if done with proper equipment. Certified collection and dismantling services are in demand from corporates who need documented disposal for their ESG reporting.

For a small business, the entry points are: (1) a certified e-waste collection service for offices and institutions; (2) a repair and refurbishment workshop; (3) a component recovery operation supplying local repairers with tested parts. All three require training, safe storage, and compliance with national e-waste regulations.

Turning Audit Data into a Business Case

Once your audit is complete, present it as a simple one-page business case: current disposal cost per month, diversion potential in kg and %, investment required (bins, scale, compost bay, training), and projected savings or revenue. Most African SMEs find that a modest segregation and composting programme pays back within 6â18 months, before counting the reputational and compliance benefits that unlock corporate and export customers.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Define audit boundary: one site, one week, all shifts.
  • â Label and separate all streams before weighing.
  • â Record weight and volume for every bag or bin.
  • â Photograph each stream and note contamination.
  • â Get current local prices from at least two recyclers.
  • â Identify all hazardous fractions and confirm licensed handlers.
  • â Set a 90-day diversion target with named responsibility.
  • â Review audit data quarterly and update the business case.

Further Reading

  • World Bank â What a Waste 2.0: A Global Snapshot of Solid Waste Management to 2050 (free PDF)
  • UNEP â Global Waste Management Outlook (free report)
  • Basel Convention â Technical Guidelines on Hazardous Waste (free)
  • UNEP â E-Waste in Africa reports and guidance (free)
  • FAO â Composting: A Practical Guide for Small-Scale Producers (free PDF)

quiz.q: What is the most common component of municipal solid waste in African cities?
quiz.explanation: Organic matter makes up 50-60% of municipal solid waste in African cities.

quiz.q: Which waste stream includes old phones and computers?
quiz.explanation: E-waste specifically refers to discarded electronic devices.

quiz.q: How long does composting typically take?
quiz.explanation: Composting organic waste usually takes 30-60 days to fully decompose.

quiz.q: Which plastic resin code is used for clear soda bottles?
quiz.explanation: PET (code 1) is clear and commonly used for beverage bottles.

quiz.q: How can you distinguish steel from aluminium?
quiz.explanation: A magnet sticks to steel but not to aluminium.

quiz.q: Which plastic is likely to crack when squeezed?
quiz.explanation: Polystyrene (PS, code 6) is brittle and cracks easily.

quiz.q: What is the first step in conducting a waste audit?
quiz.explanation: Choosing a typical day ensures the audit reflects normal waste generation.

quiz.q: In a waste audit, why should you weigh each category separately?
quiz.explanation: Separate weights allow you to calculate the percentage of each waste type.

quiz.q: What is a common hazardous waste item found in homes?
quiz.explanation: Batteries contain heavy metals and are hazardous.

quiz.q: Why should you never burn cables to recover copper?
quiz.explanation: Burning cables releases toxic fumes that harm health and the environment.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ratio of greens to browns in composting?
quiz.explanation: A 1:2 ratio of greens to browns provides the right carbon-to-nitrogen balance.

quiz.q: Which composting method uses red wiggler worms?
quiz.explanation: Vermicomposting relies on worms to break down organic waste.

quiz.q: What percentage of e-waste in Africa is formally recycled?
quiz.explanation: Only about 10-15% of Africa's e-waste is formally recycled.

quiz.q: What is a business opportunity in e-waste recycling?
quiz.explanation: Refurbishing and reselling working devices is a profitable e-waste business.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a type of waste mentioned in the module?
quiz.explanation: Nuclear waste is not covered in this module's list of waste types.

quiz.q: What tool is used to identify metals?
quiz.explanation: A magnet is a simple tool to distinguish ferrous from non-ferrous metals.

quiz.q: Which glass colour is typically lowest in recycling value?
quiz.explanation: Mixed colours lower the value because they cannot be easily separated.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of composting for soil?
quiz.explanation: Compost improves soil structure and water retention by 20-30%.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost heap?
quiz.explanation: Turning weekly aerates the pile and speeds up decomposition.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to store hazardous waste?
quiz.explanation: Sealed, labelled containers prevent leaks and accidental exposure.

quiz.q: Which of these is a hazardous warning symbol?
quiz.explanation: Skull and crossbones indicate toxic or poisonous materials.

quiz.q: What is the typical weight of waste a small restaurant might generate daily?
quiz.explanation: The example in the lesson showed 51 kg total per day.

quiz.q: Which plastic code is used for milk jugs?
quiz.explanation: HDPE (code 2) is opaque and used for milk jugs.

quiz.q: What is a key challenge of e-waste in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Most e-waste is not collected due to poor infrastructure.

quiz.q: What should you avoid composting?
quiz.explanation: Meat and bones attract pests and cause odours.

quiz.q: How much more gold is in one tonne of circuit boards compared to one tonne of gold ore?
quiz.explanation: Circuit boards contain 40-800 times more gold than gold ore.

quiz.q: What is a waste audit target example?
quiz.explanation: Setting a reduction target helps track progress.

quiz.q: Which of these is a brown material for composting?
quiz.explanation: Dry leaves are carbon-rich browns.

quiz.q: What is the first step to start an e-waste recycling business?
options: B) Set up a collection point
quiz.explanation: A collection point is the starting infrastructure for e-waste recycling.

quiz.q: What percentage of municipal waste in Africa is organic?
quiz.explanation: Organic matter typically makes up 50-60% of municipal waste.
